"Do not write anything clever," said Hemant. "Just publish."
"But it's not finished," said Maria.
"It's a weekend. One page. Your name, two projects, one link each. That's all."
"And the fonts?"
"Default. Please."
On Sunday evening Maria sent the link. "It's live," she typed to her mentors, and her hands shook slightly. By Tuesday one had replied: "Add what the project actually does in one sentence." Another: "Good start, put your email at the top."
"See?" Hemant grinned. "You would have never got those if you had waited."
Maria opened the file. "One change a month. That's my rule now."

qa.q: What did Maria send on Sunday evening?
qa.a: Maria sent the link to her mentors.

qa.q: What is Maria feeling as she sends the link?
qa.a: Maria feels nervous and exposed, since her hands shook slightly, but she does it anyway.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Maria use to grow the site, and why?
qa.a: Maria could ask one mentor to review each change before the next month, because steady feedback shows which improvements actually matter.

qa.q: How does Hemant see Maria's hesitation?
qa.a: Hemant sees perfection as the obstacle and pushes for a plain page now, then grins when replies arrive, so Hemant treats early feedback as the prize.

grounding: Shows publishing a simple portfolio quickly, sharing it for feedback, and improving it in small monthly steps.

I'm Rukmini, and last March I made a rule: one page, two projects, live by Sunday night. No custom design, just a free template and plain text.
On Saturday I wrote short blurbs for my crop-yield chart project and the library-booking tool I'd built for our hostel. On Sunday I added screenshots and links, fixed two typos, and published at 9:40 p.m. It looked plain. I sent the link to three people: my professor, a senior at a data firm, and Nirmala akka, who had mentored me in second year.
Nirmala akka replied first: 'Say what the library tool changed. How many students use it?' The senior said the charts were too small on phones.
In April I added numbers. In May I fixed the phone layout. By July it had a third project, and a recruiter found me through it.

qa.q: What time did Rukmini publish the page?
How did Rukmini probably feel sending out a site that looked plain?
qa.a: Rukmini was likely a little nervous and exposed sending something so simple, but relieved that it was finally live.

qa.q: What else could Rukmini do to keep improving the site?
qa.a: Keep asking the same few people for one comment every month, since each round of feedback led to a clear, small fix.

qa.q: How might Nirmala akka see the plain one-page site?
qa.a: Nirmala akka sees something real to comment on, and her first question pushes Rukmini to show what the tool changed.

grounding: Shows a student publishing a plain one-page site with two projects in a weekend, sharing it with mentors, and improving it month by month.

Mentoring notes – Jahnavi, alumni mentor
5 February: Disha came to our session with a plan I liked: a one-page portfolio with her two best projects, the bus-route app and the water-quality dashboard, published by Sunday. She used a basic template and turned down my urge to suggest a fancy design.
On Monday the link was in my inbox. Plain, but clear. I gave her three comments: add one sentence about who used each project, move contact details to the top, and cut the long 'about me' paragraph.
5 March: she had done all three and asked for the next round. I suggested a short write-up on one bug she fixed.
5 April: the write-up is up, and she has shared the link with two more alumni. Each month it gets a little better. I am glad she did not wait for it to be perfect.

qa.q: Which two projects were on Disha's one-page portfolio?
qa.a: The bus-route app and the water-quality dashboard.

qa.q: How does Disha seem to feel about feedback, judging by March?
qa.a: She seems open and motivated, since she made all three changes and asked for the next round herself.

qa.q: What could Disha try next to widen the feedback?
qa.a: Share the link with someone working in the field she wants, not only alumni mentors, to hear what hiring people notice.

qa.q: How does the monthly routine look from Jahnavi's side?
qa.a: Jahnavi finds it easy to help, since there is a real page to comment on each month, and is glad it was not held back for perfection.

grounding: Shows a student publishing a simple page with two projects over a weekend and improving it each month after mentor feedback.
